title: The Missing Details
preview: You're a few weeks into a new job. Your manager hands you a task without much detail -- how do you handle it when the result isn't what they expected?
setting: Your first week as a new employee, your manager stops by with a task
opener: Hey, can you prepare that report and make sure it's ready soon? Thanks!
narratorOpening: You are starting a task for your manager, a few weeks into a new job. In previous experiences, unclear instructions have led to misunderstandings and frustration on both sides. Your goal is to practice asking for what you need to get it right, instead of guessing or carrying all the blame yourself.
narratorAtmosphere: The office is quiet for now -- keyboards clicking, someone's phone buzzing a few desks away. You're still new enough that you don't yet know the unwritten rules, and Priya is already half-turned to leave.
teachingPoint: Asking clarifying questions instead of over-apologizing or getting defensive.

responseOptions.text: I don't understand your instructions, you weren't clear.
responseOptions.note: Honest, but can come across as blaming.

responseOptions.text: Sorry, I should have understood this.
responseOptions.note: Takes all the responsibility, but doesn't fix the actual problem.

responseOptions.text: Could you clarify what you'd like included, and the deadline?
responseOptions.note: Asks a clarifying question -- recommended approach.

templateEvents.text: Priya's phone buzzes on the desk. She glances at it before turning back to you.
A coworker passes by and gives Priya a quick wave, pulling her attention for a second.
The office hums on around you both for a beat before Priya glances back at her notes.
Priya's attention drifts to her screen for a moment, giving the conversation a natural pause.

missions.missionText: Priya just handed you a task without much detail, and you're not sure exactly what she wants. Figure out what you actually need to know, and ask for it before you guess wrong.

objectives.text: Respond without over-apologizing or getting defensive
Ask a clarifying question
Get a concrete detail you can use

missions.advanceWhen: The user asks a real clarifying question (about format, content, or deadline) and Priya gives a concrete answer in return.

missions.missionText: Priya's given you what you asked for. Make sure you actually have what you need, and leave the exchange on solid footing.

objectives.text: Ask a clarifying question
Get a concrete detail you can use
Confirm you understand what she needs

title: The Unexpected Conversation
preview: You're checking out at a small shop when the cashier starts chatting about the weather and her cat. Do you need something clever to say back?
setting: Checkout counter at a small local shop, right after paying
opener: Alright, you're all set! Gosh, this weather's been something lately, hasn't it?
narratorOpening: You are finishing up a purchase at a small shop. In previous experiences, casual small talk has felt confusing, like it's asking for more than you know how to give. Your goal is to practice responding in a way that's comfortable for you -- short is allowed.
narratorAtmosphere: The shop is calm, just a short line forming behind you. Dana finishes ringing up your total and looks up, in no hurry to end the conversation.
teachingPoint: Small talk doesn't require a deep or "correct" answer -- short responses are enough.

responseOptions.note: Survives the interaction but can feel uncomfortable to hold.

responseOptions.text: Honestly, small talk is hard for me to know how to respond to.
responseOptions.note: Honest, but the cashier may not know what to do with that in a checkout line.

responseOptions.text: Yeah, the weather's been nice. Hope you have a good one!
responseOptions.note: Simple, short, reciprocal -- recommended, low effort is enough.

templateEvents.text: A small line is starting to form behind you, though Dana doesn't seem to notice or mind.
The register beeps quietly as Dana straightens a stack of receipts, unhurried.
Dana glances toward the next customer in line for a moment, unbothered, still in no rush.

missions.missionText: Dana's chatting about the weather while she finishes ringing you up. You don't need anything clever -- just enough to close out the exchange comfortably.

objectives.text: Give any response, even a short one
Notice a "perfect" answer isn't needed
Leave the checkout on a comfortable note

missions.advanceWhen: The user gives at least one real response (not silence) and the exchange is naturally wrapping up -- Dana saying goodbye, ringing up the next customer, or the user signaling they're leaving.

missions.missionText: You made it through the small talk without it needing to be more than it was. See the checkout out to a natural close.

objectives.text: Give any response, even a short one
Notice a "perfect" answer isn't needed
End the interaction warmly, on your own terms

title: Too Much Happening at Once
preview: It's your first haircut in ages, and the salon is loud and busy. How do you handle it when the noise starts to feel like too much?
setting: A hair salon, first haircut in a long time -- hairdryers running and other conversations happening nearby
opener: So, are we thinking just a trim today, or switching things up a bit?
narratorOpening: You are visiting a new stylist today. In previous experiences, staying in a loud, crowded space for a while has been hard to manage without feeling overwhelmed. Your goal is to practice noticing what you need and speaking up before it becomes too much.
narratorAtmosphere: The salon is crowded. People are talking, a hair dryer is running nearby, other customers are waiting, and Marcus turns toward you, scissors in hand, ready to start.
teachingPoint: Noticing sensory overload early and asking for what you need before it becomes too much.

responseOptions.text: Just a trim is fine, thanks.
responseOptions.note: Pushes through the sensory overload -- finishes the haircut, but exhausting.

responseOptions.text: Actually, I need to go, sorry.
responseOptions.note: Protects you right now, but avoids the situation instead of addressing it.

responseOptions.text: The noise is overwhelming -- could we keep it quieter, fewer questions?
responseOptions.note: Names the need directly -- recommended, gives the stylist a chance to adjust.

templateEvents.text: The shop gets even busier -- another hairdryer clicks on nearby.
Marcus cracks a small joke about Mondays, half to you and half to the room.
Jamie, in the next chair, leans over with a grin: "First cut in a while too? I feel that."
Jamie chimes in on your conversation with Marcus: "Honestly, I always just tell them 'surprise me' and hope for the best."
The shop quiets for a moment -- the buzz of the clippers fills the space. Marcus focuses on the cut, comfortable letting the silence sit.
For a beat, the only sound is the snip of scissors -- Marcus is focused on getting the cut right.

missions.missionText: The salon is loud, and it's already a lot -- clippers, other conversations, hair dryers. Notice what you need before it becomes too much, and let Marcus know.

objectives.text: Get through the opening small talk about the cut
Notice when it starts to feel like too much
Say something to Marcus about what you need

missions.advanceWhen: The user clearly communicates a specific need or discomfort related to the noise/environment (not just tolerating it silently), and Marcus responds to it.

missions.missionText: Marcus knows what's going on now. See if the adjustment actually helps, and let him know either way.

objectives.text: Notice when it starts to feel like too much
Say something to Marcus about what you need
Check in on whether it's actually better now

title: Asking for a Change
preview: Ms. Alvarez is mid-lecture on ethos, pathos, and logos, and the overhead lights are too bright to focus. Do you interrupt the class to say something?
setting: Classroom, mid-lecture on ethos, pathos, and logos -- the overhead lights are uncomfortably bright
opener: ...and that's pathos, the emotional appeal. Now, logos: this is where your evidence and reasoning come in, the actual facts backing up your claim. So if ethos is "trust me," and pathos is "feel this," logos is "here's the proof." Let's look at how a writer might layer all three in the same paragraph --
narratorOpening: You're sitting through a lecture on ethos, pathos, and logos -- the three classical appeals -- and the overhead lights are uncomfortably bright today, making it hard to concentrate. In previous experiences, interrupting a class already in progress has felt like way too much attention to draw on yourself. Your goal is to practice speaking up mid-lesson when you need to, even though it feels like interrupting.
narratorAtmosphere: Ms. Alvarez is at the whiteboard, marker in hand, diagramming the three appeals as she talks. The rest of the room is quiet and focused, pens moving, eyes on the board -- and the overhead lights buzz and glare more than usual today.
teachingPoint: Self-advocacy -- it's okay to interrupt when you need to, even mid-lesson.

responseOptions.note: Draws attention by speaking up, then backs away before naming the actual need -- the problem stays unaddressed.

responseOptions.text: Sorry, but the lights are really bright.
responseOptions.note: Interrupts and names the frustration, but doesn't say what would help.

responseOptions.text: Sorry to interrupt -- could we dim the lights? They're really bright.
responseOptions.note: Interrupts respectfully with a specific, reasonable request -- recommended, gives the teacher something to act on right away.

templateEvents.text: Ms. Alvarez's marker squeaks against the whiteboard as she underlines a word, a couple of classmates glancing up to copy it down.
A classmate near you shifts in their seat and flips to a new page, pen scratching as they keep taking notes.
Ms. Alvarez taps her marker against the board, giving the room a beat before continuing the lesson.
For a moment, the only sound is Ms. Alvarez's marker squeaking against the whiteboard as she keeps writing.

missions.missionText: Ms. Alvarez is mid-lecture and the lights are too bright to focus. Interrupting class feels like a big deal, but you need something to change.

objectives.text: Get her attention without waiting for a pause that won't come
Name specifically what's bothering you
Ask for something she can act on

missions.advanceWhen: The user interrupts and names a specific, actionable request (not just discomfort in general), and Ms. Alvarez responds to it.

missions.missionText: Ms. Alvarez adjusted things for you. Make sure the rest of class actually works now that you've spoken up.

objectives.text: Name specifically what's bothering you
Ask for something she can act on
Settle back into the lesson without it feeling like a bigger deal than it needed to be
